title: Cyrus and the Summer
premise: Wren Halloran has spent ten years rebuilding her life around her daughter and the failing bookshop she inherited, never expecting the orchard deed left by her late grandmother to name Cyrus Vance—the man who walked out of her life a decade ago—as co-owner. Cyrus returns to the town of Alder Creek to sell his half and fund his father's care, forcing them into weeks of shared labor restoring the orchard while the bakery below Wren's shop faces eviction. As old letters surface revealing that Wren's grandmother deliberately entangled their names to give them a second chance, both must confront how power—Cyrus's family money, Wren's quiet stubbornness—corrupted what they once had. In the end, Cyrus chooses belonging over leverage, they save the bakery together, and Wren finally says the rehearsed sentence: 'I never stopped choosing you.'
about_author: Vesper Ishikawa is a former orchard worker turned novelist who writes love stories set in small towns where land holds memory. They live between seasons, splitting the year between a coastal bookshop and a family farm.

chapters.title: The Deed That Wouldn't Die
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. While sorting her grandmother's papers above the bookshop, Wren discovers the orchard deed names Cyrus Vance as co-heir—a name she hasn't spoken in ten years. The emotional beat is dread wrapped in disbelief, as the past arrives on stamped legal paper.

chapters.title: A Man at the Register
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus arrives in Alder Creek intending to sign papers and leave within a week, but his first stop is the bookshop, where he finds Wren mid-shift. The beat is charged awkwardness—two people performing indifference badly.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Over coffee neither drinks, they agree to split the orchard's maintenance costs until it can be sold. Wren hides that the bakery lease expires in September; Cyrus hides his father's mounting care bills. The beat is mutual concealment dressed as civility.

chapters.title: What the Trees Remember
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Walking the overgrown orchard, Cyrus recalls the summer he and Wren planted the north row together. A storm forces them into the shed, and proximity cracks his composure. The beat is nostalgia weaponized against him.

chapters.title: The Bakery Clock
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Her daughter Juniper befriends Cyrus at story hour, unaware of history. Wren receives the bakery's final lease notice and says nothing to Cyrus. The beat is the loneliness of carrying a deadline alone.

chapters.title: Letters in the Wall
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Repairing the shed wall, Cyrus finds a tin of letters from Wren's grandmother to his late mother—evidence the two women engineered the deed together. He pockets one letter instead of showing Wren. The beat is temptation and small betrayal.

chapters.title: Harvest Hands
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The first apple harvest forces real collaboration; muscle memory of working beside Cyrus unsettles her more than any argument could. Juniper asks why Cyrus looks at her mom 'like a book he already read.' The beat is warmth sneaking past defenses.

chapters.title: The Vance Name
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. His brother arrives from the city pressuring him to liquidate fast and cut costs—including abandoning the orchard. Cyrus realizes his family's wealth always decided things for him. The beat is the theme of power surfacing as inheritance.

chapters.title: Rain on Tin
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Trapped overnight in the orchard house by a storm, Wren and Cyrus nearly say everything and instead argue about who left whom. She almost speaks the rehearsed sentence and swallows it. The beat is aching near-miss.

chapters.title: The Pocketed Letter
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Wren discovers the missing letter and accuses Cyrus of manipulating her again—of using information as leverage, like his family always did. Trust fractures. The beat is righteous anger masking heartbreak.

chapters.title: Juniper's Question
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Juniper, sensing tension, asks if Cyrus is leaving 'like before.' Wren must explain abandonment without bitterness and fails halfway through. The beat is a mother confronting what her silence has cost her daughter.

chapters.title: Cold Storage
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus signs preliminary sale papers with a developer, then walks the empty orchard at night and cannot do it. He tears up the draft—but tells no one. The beat is private conversion, invisible to Wren.

chapters.title: The Town Meeting
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At a public hearing about the orchard's future, the developer reveals Cyrus's signed intent. Wren learns of his reversal only when he stands and publicly refuses the sale, humiliating his brother. The beat is vindication arriving too late to feel clean.

chapters.title: What Power Buys
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. His brother threatens to seize their father's care arrangements unless Cyrus sells. Cyrus sees plainly how money has corrupted every relationship he has. The beat is the novel's thematic crux: power as isolation.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren admits to her best friend that for ten years she has rehearsed one sentence she never got to say. Her friend challenges her: rehearsed words are armor, not truth. The beat is preparation meeting fear.

chapters.title: Blight
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternate. A blight hits the north row—the trees they planted together. Working side by side to save them, they speak honestly for the first time: why he left, why she let him believe she wanted him gone. The beat is confession without resolution.

chapters.title: Lease's End
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The bakery lease expires; the landlord locks the door. Cyrus offers to buy the building outright, and Wren refuses—she won't be rescued by his money again. The beat is pride colliding with love, both justified.

chapters.title: The Grandmother's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Cyrus finally gives Wren the letter he kept: her grandmother wrote that she entangled their names because 'some debts are paid in staying, not in leaving.' Wren weeps—not for the scheme, but for being seen. The beat is grief transmuted into permission.

chapters.title: The Offer Refused, Then Remade
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren counters: not charity, partnership—Cyrus invests as an equal owner of the bookshop-bakery, with terms she writes. He signs without reading twice. The beat is power rebalanced into trust.

chapters.title: The Sentence Spoken
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POVs. On the last night before Cyrus was scheduled to leave, under the saved north row, Wren finally says the sentence: 'I never stopped choosing you.' Cyrus answers with his own decade-old unfinished reply. The beat is release after long suspension.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Harvest
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later: the bakery reopens beneath the bookshop, Cyrus's father moves to Alder Creek, and the orchard yields its first full harvest. The beat is quiet abundance—belonging made ordinary.

chapters.title: Cyrus and the Summer
chapters.summary: Cyrus's POV. Closing mirror of chapter one: Cyrus adds his own paper to the tin in the wall—a new deed amendment naming all three of them, plus a letter for whoever finds it. The beat is memory chosen forward, legacy rewritten.
